title: Neagle, Debs, Midwest Oil, and Dames & Moore: inherent power and historical practice
shortTitle: Neagle, Debs, Midwest Oil, and Dames & Moore: inherent power and historical practice
summary: Earlier executive-power cases illustrate protection of federal functions, emergency litigation, stewardship of federal land, and congressional acquiescence in foreign claims settlements.
notes:
The assigned comparison asks how earlier recognitions of executive authority fit Youngstown. In re Neagle involved a deputy marshal prosecuted by California after killing a man he believed threatened Justice Field. The Court treated protection of the Justice as part of faithful execution even without an express bodyguard statute. In re Debs upheld executive resort to an injunction against interference with interstate railway commerce during the Pullman strike, despite the absence of specific authorization to seek that labor injunction. The editors qualify their account of the institutional consequences: contempt enforcement also affected the practical availability of a jury trial.

United States v. Midwest Oil upheld withdrawal of federal lands from oil exploration despite statutory language opening the tracts. The account relies on the history of similar withdrawals known to Congress to explain implied authority to preserve Congress’s property interests pending legislative reconsideration. Historical practice does work only when its content and Congress’s relationship to it support the inference; a general assertion of national need does not automatically place an action within this reasoning.

Dames & Moore v. Regan concerned measures implementing the Iranian hostage settlement, including suspension of domestic litigation and referral of claims to an international tribunal. The excerpt distinguishes measures supported by express emergency-economic legislation from the litigation suspension, for which it identifies a history of congressionally accepted presidential claims settlements and an absence of subsequent legislative resistance. The Court reserved possible compensation claims if the tribunal furnished materially less relief. These are substantial editorial case accounts; no full opinions or complete procedural histories appear in this assigned passage.
